content: 1. Parenting interventions should be integrated into national and/or subnational government financing plans to ensure sustainable implementation and support. 2. In humanitarian settings where clear budget lines are absent, a combination of development funding for research and humanitarian funding for implementation may be necessary to facilitate the delivery of parenting interventions. 3. During the adaptation and implementation of guidelines, human resource management is critical. Workforce resources must be carefully planned to minimize the burden on delivery staff. This includes allocating sufficient time for staff to prepare and conduct parenting interventions as part of their duties and providing adequate support to maintain fidelity to the program. 4. Staff responsible for delivering parenting programs must receive appropriate training, deployment, and ongoing support to ensure effective implementation. 5. Curricula, teaching, and learning materials used in parenting interventions should be as current and evidence-based as possible to maximize their effectiveness. 6. The implementation of parenting programs should be designed with scalability in mind. Scaling up these programs typically requires the endorsement of local administrators and government policymakers, effective leadership to drive process transformation, and the training of relevant workers and supervisors. 7. Collaboration with multiple stakeholders and partners is essential to strengthen implementation and sustain progress. Working across various sectors can help ensure a comprehensive, cross-sectoral, and sustainable approach. 8. Sustainable financial support sources must be identified to maintain the long-term viability of parenting interventions. 9. The context in which a program is implemented should be carefully considered, as it may influence the program's delivery and effectiveness. Programs should be tailored to fit the needs of different populations living in diverse contexts. 10. Monitoring and evaluation mechanisms should be incorporated into the implementation process to facilitate ongoing data collection and analysis. This ensures that programs are being carried out as planned, problems are identified and addressed promptly, and feedback is provided to managers and staff. 11. Data collected during monitoring should be processed and analyzed promptly, with results communicated to those in positions to take corrective action. 12. The World Health Organization (WHO) will use routine surveys to assess how parenting recommendations are integrated into national policies and training courses. WHO will also collaborate with national authorities to include questions about the new recommendations and workforce experiences in integrating these into routine national training assessments and supervisory structures. 13. Local adaptation of the guidelines will be supported through WHO country offices and ministries of health. National guidelines related to child health, development, care, parenting support, or violence prevention will be reviewed to integrate relevant approaches. 14. The current guideline will be disseminated via the WHO website and through a broad network of international partners, including WHO country and regional offices, ministries of health, collaborating centers, universities, other United Nations agencies, and non-governmental organizations. 15. Reviews of the guideline are expected to be published in peer-reviewed journals to ensure transparency and accessibility of findings. 16. The WHO Steering Group will continue to monitor research developments in parenting and child maltreatment prevention, particularly in areas where the quality of evidence is low or very low. If an update to the guideline is warranted (likely five years after publication), WHO will coordinate the update following formal procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. 17. As the guideline approaches its five-year review period, WHO and its partners will conduct a search for new evidence and welcome suggestions for additional questions to evaluate during the review process. 18. The WHO guidelines on parenting interventions aim to prevent maltreatment and enhance parent-child relationships for children aged 0–17 years. These guidelines are informed by systematic reviews of evidence and are designed to support global efforts to improve child well-being and family dynamics.
